New Orleans. A major port city at the mouth of the Mississippi River in southeastern Louisiana, founded by the French in seventeen eighteen. Its unique cultural identity emerged from the collision of French, Spanish, African, and American influences, creating a distinctly polyglot urban society unlike anywhere else in North America.

Founded as La Nouvelle-Orléans by French colonists in seventeen eighteen, the city was transferred to Spanish rule from seventeen sixty-three to eighteen oh-three, then purchased by the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of eighteen oh-three.

Developed as a major Atlantic port despite its swampy, hurricane-prone location, the city's geography forced architectural and social innovation including raised architecture and complex drainage systems. Enslaved African labor built the city's economy. The slave trade dominated commerce, and slavery remained embedded in daily life longer than elsewhere in the United States.

The city's unique demographic makeup included free people of color, Creoles descended from French and Spanish and African ancestry, and immigrants from throughout the Atlantic world.

Jazz emerged from New Orleans' African, Caribbean, and European musical traditions, nurtured in dance halls, churches, and street parades beginning in the early twentieth century. Louis Armstrong and other jazz pioneers made New Orleans synonymous with the music that would define American culture globally. Jazz was born here and nowhere else.

The city's French Quarter, known as Vieux Carré, preserves colonial architecture and street culture unlike any other American city. It remains the cultural and tourist heart of New Orleans.

The city was devastated by Hurricane Katrina in twenty oh-five, exposing deep racial and economic inequalities. Recovery remains ongoing and incomplete, with continuing debates over gentrification.
